Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- Over 28,000 Liverpool fans marked the 20th anniversary of the Hillsborough disaster in a special memorial service at Anfield on Wednesday. Liverpool supporters at the Kop end paid their respects in an emotional afternoon at Anfield. A total of 96 supporters died on April 15, 1989 before the FA Cup semifinal between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest at Sheffield Wednesday's stadium, the worst-ever tragedy in English sporting history. To commemorate the anniversary, the city of Liverpool came to a standstill at 3.06 pm (1406 GMT) with the bells of the two cathedrals and its civic buildings ringing out in memory of those fans who lost their lives. On Anfield's famous Kop, 96 candles were lit while commemorations took place at Hillsborough and also in Nottingham. Members of the current Liverpool team stood somberly as hymns were played before a roll call of the dead was read out. Club legend Kenny Dalglish, who was Liverpool manager at the time of the disaster, then read a short prayer. The mayor of Liverpool, Steve Rotherham, who was at the game 20 years ago, helped organize the emotional memorial. "Hillsborough affected so many lives, not just on Merseyside but across the whole of the UK," he said. "I attended the match 20 years ago and the passing years do not diminish the importance and the poignancy of this occasion." Liverpool captain Steven Gerrard, whose 10-year-old cousin Jon-Paul Gilhooley was the youngest victim of the tragedy, spoke of his feelings this week. "Time has gone by, but the scars will never ever be healed and the fans will never ever forget. So you can always rely on our supporters to be there for you when you need them." The Liverpool fans died in a crush which started just before the kick-off as the gate at the Leppings Lane End was opened with terrible consequences. The match started but when the scale of the tragedy became clear, it was swiftly abandoned at 3.06 pm. In the immediate aftermath, the British government commissioned Lord Justice Taylor to conduct an inquiry which would have a far-reaching impact on football. Taylor was deeply critical of the police operation at Hillsborough, but his most significant recommendations were the removal of perimeter fencing and the creation of all-seater stadia. His report also cleared Liverpool fans of blame for the tragedy after lurid tabloid headlines provoked revulsion on Merseyside. Prime minister Gordon Brown paid reference to the controversy in an interview released on Liverpool's official television channel. "It was wrong for people to blame, as some did, Liverpool fans on that day," he said. "That's probably what matters most -- that people understood that the behavior of Liverpool fans in helping each other was magnificent. "Let's never forget the fans who cruelly lost their lives on a day when we know the people of Liverpool were trying to help each other," he added. However, the people of Liverpool are still angry and bitter at the lack of justice for those who died -- and that frustration surfaced when Andy Burnham, the   Secretary of State for Culture, Media and Sport took to the stand to address the crowd. As Burnham spoke, the crowd rose as one to sing "Justice for the 96". The Kop chant boomed around the stadium and Burnham, an Everton fan, was left in no doubt about the strength of feeling over the lack of accountability from officialdom over the tragedy. Fittingly, the ceremony was concluded with Gerry Marsden leading the fans in singing Liverpool anthem 'You'll Never Walk Alone'.

(CNN) — More than 28,000 Liverpool supporters gathered at Anfield on Wednesday for a special service commemorating 20 years since the Hillsborough disaster. The afternoon was deeply emotional, particularly at the Kop end, where fans honored those who died.

On April 15, 1989, 96 Liverpool supporters lost their lives before the FA Cup semifinal against Nottingham Forest at Sheffield Wednesday’s ground. It remains the deadliest tragedy in the history of English sport.

At 3:06 p.m. (1406 GMT), Liverpool paused to remember the victims. Bells rang from the city’s two cathedrals and civic buildings, while 96 candles were illuminated on Anfield’s famous Kop. Memorial events were also held at Hillsborough and in Nottingham.

Liverpool’s current players stood in solemn silence as hymns were performed and the names of all those who died were read aloud. Kenny Dalglish, the club icon who was Liverpool’s manager when the disaster occurred, followed with a brief prayer.

The moving ceremony was partly organized by Liverpool Mayor Steve Rotherham, who had attended the match two decades earlier.

“Hillsborough affected so many lives, not just on Merseyside but across the whole of the UK,” he said. “I attended the match 20 years ago and the passing years do not diminish the importance and the poignancy of this occasion.”

Liverpool captain Steven Gerrard also spoke during the week about the tragedy. His cousin, 10-year-old Jon-Paul Gilhooley, was the youngest person to die.

“Time has gone by, but the scars will never ever be healed and the fans will never ever forget,” Gerrard said. “So you can always rely on our supporters to be there for you when you need them.”

The fatal crush began shortly before kickoff after a gate at the Leppings Lane End was opened, with devastating results. Although play initially got underway, the match was quickly stopped at 3:06 p.m. once the seriousness of the situation became apparent.

In the period immediately following the disaster, the British government appointed Lord Justice Taylor to lead an investigation whose conclusions would transform football. Taylor strongly criticized the policing at Hillsborough. Among his most consequential proposals were the removal of perimeter fences and the conversion of stadiums into all-seater venues.

The Taylor report also found that Liverpool supporters were not responsible for what happened, countering sensational tabloid accusations that had caused widespread outrage across Merseyside.

Prime Minister Gordon Brown addressed that controversy in an interview broadcast on Liverpool’s official television channel.

“It was wrong for people to blame, as some did, Liverpool fans on that day,” he said. “That’s probably what matters most—that people understood that the behavior of Liverpool fans in helping each other was magnificent.”

“Let’s never forget the fans who cruelly lost their lives on a day when we know the people of Liverpool were trying to help each other,” Brown added.

Nevertheless, anger and resentment remain in Liverpool over what many see as a failure to deliver justice for the victims. Those feelings became clear when Andy Burnham, the Secretary of State for Culture, Media and Sport, stepped forward to speak.

As he addressed the gathering, the entire crowd stood and began singing, “Justice for the 96.” The chant echoed powerfully around Anfield, making the depth of frustration over the absence of official accountability unmistakable to Burnham, who is an Everton supporter.

The memorial ended appropriately with Gerry Marsden leading the crowd in a rendition of Liverpool’s anthem, “You’ll Never Walk Alone.”

**LIVERPOOL, England (CNN)** — Thousands of people filled Liverpool’s Anfield stadium Wednesday to mark the 20th anniversary of the Hillsborough disaster, one of the darkest days in British sporting history.

The memorial service honored the 96 Liverpool supporters who died after a crush developed at Sheffield’s Hillsborough stadium during an FA Cup semifinal against Nottingham Forest on April 15, 1989.

At 3:06 p.m. — the time the match was stopped — the crowd observed two minutes of silence. Church bells rang across Liverpool, while shops and public buildings also paused in remembrance.

Inside Anfield, the names of the victims were read aloud as relatives, survivors, supporters and members of Liverpool Football Club gathered beneath banners calling for justice. Ninety-six candles were lit in their memory.

Liverpool players and staff joined the service, and club captain Steven Gerrard, whose cousin Jon-Paul Gilhooley was the youngest victim at age 10, was among those paying tribute.

The ceremony also reflected the continuing anger of many families over the handling of the disaster and its aftermath. When government minister Andy Burnham addressed the stadium, parts of the crowd responded with chants of “Justice for the 96.”

The 1989 crush occurred in overcrowded standing pens at the Leppings Lane end of Hillsborough. An official inquiry later identified failures in police crowd control as the main cause and led to major safety reforms at British football grounds.

For Liverpool, Wednesday’s commemoration was both a public act of remembrance and a reminder that, two decades later, many families still believed they had not received a full accounting of what happened.

The service ended with the crowd singing Liverpool’s anthem, **“You’ll Never Walk Alone.”**

## Hillsborough’s 20th anniversary — 15 April 2009

Liverpool marked the 20th anniversary of the Hillsborough disaster with its largest memorial service since 1989. At the time, the death toll was commemorated as 96; it was formally revised to 97 after Andrew Devine’s death was ruled in 2021 to have resulted from his Hillsborough injuries.

### Memorial service at Anfield

More than 30,000 people filled Anfield, with the Kop becoming the focus of remembrance. Bereaved families and survivors were joined by Liverpool supporters, former players and managers, and the club’s first-team squad, led by manager Rafael Benítez and captain Steven Gerrard. Representatives of Everton and other parts of football also attended.

The service included:

- The reading of the names of all 96 victims.
- The lighting of candles and the laying of wreaths.
- A two-minute silence beginning at **3:06 p.m.**, the time the 1989 FA Cup semifinal was stopped.
- Prayers and an address led by the Bishop of Liverpool, the Right Reverend James Jones.
- A concluding rendition of **“You’ll Never Walk Alone,”** led by Gerry Marsden and sung by the crowd.

Former Liverpool figures, including Kenny Dalglish—who had managed the club in 1989 and had attended many victims’ funerals—joined the families and supporters. The presence of the current team carried particular meaning for Gerrard, whose ten-year-old cousin, Jon-Paul Gilhooley, was the youngest person killed.

### “Justice for the 96”

The most politically significant moment came during an address by Culture Secretary **Andy Burnham**, representing the government. As he began speaking, sections of the crowd interrupted him with chants of:

> “Justice for the 96.”

Burnham acknowledged that the families had waited too long for the full story and said the government remained committed to helping. The reaction demonstrated that the anniversary was not regarded simply as an occasion for mourning: families and supporters still wanted disclosure of official records, accountability, and correction of the false allegations made against Liverpool supporters after the disaster.

The experience had a lasting effect on Burnham. He subsequently pressed the issue within government, helping to set in motion the creation later in 2009 of the **Hillsborough Independent Panel**, chaired by Bishop James Jones. Its 2012 report exposed the scale of official failures and the alteration of police statements.

**Margaret Aspinall**, speaking for the Hillsborough Family Support Group and as the mother of victim James Aspinall, stressed the families’ continuing campaign for truth and justice. Her contribution reinforced the central message that remembrance could not be separated from the demand for accountability.

### Tributes across Liverpool

At 3:06 p.m., much of Liverpool came to a standstill:

- Civic buildings lowered flags to half-mast.
- Church and civic bells tolled **96 times**.
- Public transport paused and people observed the silence in workplaces, shops and streets.
- Wreaths and scarves were placed at memorials, while supporters gathered at Anfield and elsewhere in the city.

Tributes were also held in Sheffield and at football grounds around the country. The commemorations combined grief, solidarity and protest: the victims were remembered individually, the survivors and families were supported publicly, and the chant “Justice for the 96” made clear that, 20 years later, Liverpool did not consider the Hillsborough story closed.

# Anfield falls silent as more than 28,000 remember Hillsborough victims

**LIVERPOOL —** More than 28,000 supporters gathered at Anfield for an emotional ceremony marking the 25th anniversary of the Hillsborough disaster, filling Liverpool’s stadium with scarves, banners and flowers as the city remembered the 96 men, women and children who died.

Families of the victims sat alongside survivors, players, club officials, politicians and representatives of Liverpool’s footballing rivals for the memorial service on 15 April 2014. Across the stadium, the names of those who lost their lives were displayed and read aloud, each one met with solemn attention from the crowd.

At 3.06pm — the time the 1989 FA Cup semi-final was halted at Hillsborough — Anfield fell silent. The pause was observed across Liverpool and at other locations around the country, bringing traffic, workplaces and public buildings to a standstill.

The silence inside the ground was broken only by the faint sound of birds and the movement of flags in the wind. Many supporters bowed their heads; others held one another or wiped away tears. Relatives carried photographs of loved ones, while red-and-white scarves were draped over seats and barriers throughout the stadium.

The ceremony recalled the events of 15 April 1989, when overcrowding in the Leppings Lane terrace at Sheffield Wednesday’s Hillsborough ground led to a fatal crush during Liverpool’s semi-final against Nottingham Forest. Ninety-six people were recognised at the time as having died as a result of the disaster. The official death toll was increased to 97 in 2021 following the death of Andrew Devine, who had suffered life-changing injuries at Hillsborough.

A large display on the Kop paid tribute to the victims and marked a quarter of a century since the tragedy. The number 96, long a symbol of remembrance and of the families’ campaign for justice, was visible throughout the ground.

Liverpool manager Brendan Rodgers and Everton manager Roberto Martínez were among those who addressed the service, underlining the solidarity shown across Merseyside. Everton’s presence drew warm applause, reflecting the support the club and its followers had repeatedly offered to bereaved families and survivors.

Martínez spoke of the shared grief of the two clubs and of the responsibility to ensure that the victims were never forgotten. Rodgers paid tribute to the dignity and determination of the families, whose campaign had challenged the original account of the disaster and fought for the truth for more than two decades.

Margaret Aspinall, chairwoman of the Hillsborough Family Support Group, delivered one of the ceremony’s most moving speeches. Her 18-year-old son, James, was among those killed. She thanked supporters for standing with the families and spoke of the long struggle to correct the record of what happened.

The anniversary came at a particularly significant moment. Fresh inquests into the deaths had recently begun in Warrington after the original inquest verdicts were quashed. That development followed the 2012 report of the Hillsborough Independent Panel, which exposed serious failures by the authorities and the subsequent alteration or suppression of evidence.

The panel’s findings confirmed that supporters had not been responsible for the disaster and revealed the extent to which police statements had been changed. They also highlighted failures in crowd control, emergency planning and the medical response.

For many inside Anfield, the memorial was therefore not only an act of remembrance but also a public reaffirmation of the demand for accountability.

The service included prayers, readings and music, with candles lit in memory of the victims. The crowd joined in hymns before the ceremony closed with Liverpool’s anthem, **“You’ll Never Walk Alone.”** Its familiar words carried around the stadium as supporters raised scarves above their heads.

Outside Anfield, the club’s Hillsborough memorial was covered with flowers, handwritten messages, football shirts and photographs. Tributes had arrived from across Britain and overseas, including from rival clubs whose supporters set aside sporting loyalties to stand with Liverpool.

The atmosphere combined deep sorrow with quiet defiance. The anniversary reopened painful memories for survivors and families, but it also demonstrated the strength of a campaign sustained through years of official resistance and public misunderstanding.

As the crowd slowly left the stadium, many stopped again at the memorial. Some touched the engraved names; others stood in silence.

Twenty-five years after the disaster, Anfield’s message remained clear: the victims would be remembered individually, the survivors would be supported, and the pursuit of truth and justice would continue.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the events surrounding Liverpool’s 20th-anniversary Hillsborough memorial, while also explaining the disaster, the Taylor inquiry, and the continuing campaign for justice.
counterfactuals.output:
Liverpool marked the 20th anniversary of the Hillsborough disaster on 15 April 2009 with a memorial service at Anfield attended by tens of thousands of supporters, survivors, players, officials and relatives of those who died. At 3:06 p.m.—the time the 1989 match was stopped—the stadium observed a two-minute silence. Ninety-six candles were lit, one for each person then officially counted among the dead, and the names of the victims were read aloud. Government minister Andy Burnham’s address was repeatedly met with chants of “Justice for the 96,” reflecting families’ anger that key records remained undisclosed and no one had been held properly accountable. Burnham promised to press for the release of official documents.

The disaster occurred during the FA Cup semi-final between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest at Sheffield Wednesday’s Hillsborough stadium on 15 April 1989. Severe congestion developed outside the Leppings Lane end. Police opened an exit gate but failed to direct arriving supporters away from already overcrowded central standing pens. The resulting crush killed 94 people that day; two later died from their injuries. Andrew Devine, who suffered catastrophic injuries, died in 2021 and was legally recognized as the 97th victim. Claims that drunken or ticketless Liverpool fans caused the disaster were false and were amplified by hostile policing accounts and notorious press coverage.

Lord Justice Taylor’s official inquiry concluded that the principal cause was a failure of police control. It criticized stadium design, crowd-management arrangements and the emergency response, and its recommendations led to major safety reforms, notably all-seater grounds in the top divisions. Nevertheless, families believed the inquiry had not delivered accountability. The original inquests returned “accidental death” verdicts and imposed a controversial 3:15 p.m. cutoff, effectively excluding evidence about much of the emergency response.

The anniversary therefore served both as remembrance and protest. Campaign groups and bereaved families continued to demand full disclosure, new inquests and responsibility for the police and other authorities. Their efforts later produced the Hillsborough Independent Panel’s 2012 report, which exposed extensive official failings and the alteration of police statements. The original inquest verdicts were quashed, and in 2016 a new jury found that the victims had been unlawfully killed and that supporter behavior had not contributed to the disaster. Despite that vindication, the limited success of subsequent prosecutions meant that the campaign for full accountability continued.
